title: The HQIM Farce
author: Daniel OK-Carr
summary: Daniel OK-Carr, a classroom teacher, argues that the high-quality instructional materials (HQIM) label gives districts false assurance about the basal reading programs they buy. Using Savvas myView, which was rebranded in 2025 as Science of Reading aligned, he reports that the revamped student book is essentially the 2020 book with the worksheets reordered. He shows how its knowledge building units bundle unrelated texts, from Angel Island interrogations to Martian microbiology, under a loose theme, and how the optional online library lets it earn a green EdReports mark. He then walks through a single week of lessons built on a text called Patterns in Nature, which gets basic botany, entomology and mathematics wrong and asks eight-year-olds to hunt for context clues to the word colorful. The close reading routine of highlighting every page fills two days of the week and leaves little time for actual reading. He concludes that the gatekeepers who certify such products need to be replaced and that HQIM is meaningless until it is better defined, while noting that good ELA curricula do exist.
points: A rebranded Science of Reading edition of myView changed only the order of the worksheets, so the HQIM stamp tells purchasers little about whether the content improved.
Knowledge building units can earn a green EdReports mark while bundling unrelated texts, because an optional online library is counted toward the criterion.
A single week of lessons on Patterns in Nature shows factual errors in biology and mathematics getting past every content editor, which undercuts the claim of rigorous informational text.

The mandated close reading routine of highlighting and underlining every page consumes two days a week and replaces sustained reading, so students rarely read a whole book across grades three to five.
The author's remedy is better curriculum gatekeeping and a tighter definition of HQIM, not abandoning high-quality curriculum, which he says exists.
quotes: I bought the 2020 student textbook for my grade level to see the differences myself. What changed? I kid you not, the order of the worksheets.

Under this definition of knowledge building, I am reasonably confident I could go into my school library, randomly grab five different books from various genres, concoct some creative thematic connection, and call it a unit.

But to do this I had to dedicate hours upon hours of personal time, raid the library storage room for class sets of books (the 3rd through 5th grade curriculum has students read 0 whole books over 3 years), and generally apply a liberal interpretation of our 4 grade pacing guide.

If a curriculum claims to build background knowledge through “complex informational text”, at minimum that text should be scientifically and mathematically accurate. Somehow, in the very first text, it failed on both accounts.
These aren’t pattern in nature. These are artificial human arrangements using items gathered from a backyard.
Colorful. COLORFUL. We are asking eight- and nine-year-olds to hunt for context clues to determine the meaning of the word colorful.

Parents don’t know. Policy makers don’t know. It’s not until you are staring a class of glassy-eyed third graders, highlighters in hand, dully marking up texts day after day do you fully understand the tragedy of the situation and experience the searing rage that teachers across the country feel as they are forced to feed students a steady diet of this rotten basal stew.
Until we have a better definition of High-Quality Instructional Materials, relying on HQIM to improve education in this country is a fool’s errand.
